question: Which PEP proposed making the CPython global interpreter lock optional?

subquestions: Which PEP proposed making the CPython Global Interpreter Lock (GIL) optional?

args.query: PEP make the CPython global interpreter lock optional
PEP make the CPython global interpreter lock optional

observations.content:
[1] Global interpreter lock - Wikipedia
    https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Global_interpreter_lock
    In Python 3.13, an experimental "free-threaded" build of CPython was introduced as part of PEP 703 – Making the Global Interpreter Lock Optional in CPython. This build allows developers to compile Python without the Global Interpreter Lock (GIL)...

[2] PEP 703: Making the Python global interpreter lock optional
    https://lwn.net/Articles/919563/
    The global interpreter lock will remain the default for CPython builds and python.org downloads. A new build configuration flag, --without-gil will be added to the configure script that will build CPython without the global interpreter lock.

[3] PEP 703 – Making the Global Interpreter Lock Optional in CPython
    https://www.linkedin.com/posts/eliot-kmiec_pep-703-making-the-global-interpreter-lock-activity-7271941402740043776-IS5w
    The Global Interpreter Lock (GIL) is now optional, unlocking real multi-core parallelism in pure Python. For decades, the GIL limited Python to a single thread, forcing teams to rely on multiprocessing or external frameworks for CPU-bound workloads.

[4] The GIL Was Removed From Python!? – SuperFastPython
    https://superfastpython.com/gil-removed-from-python/
    -- PEP 703 – Making the Global Interpreter Lock Optional in CPython. These are provisional plans. Plans can change. There are other concerns too, once we start disabling the GIL in Python 3.13.

[5] Faster Python: Unlocking the Python Global Interpreter Lock - The...
    https://blog.jetbrains.com/pycharm/2025/07/faster-python-unlocking-the-python-global-interpreter-lock/
    “Global Interpreter Lock” (or “GIL”) is a familiar term in the Python community. It is a well-known Python feature. But what exactly is a GIL?You can check out PEP 703 – Making the Global Interpreter Lock Optional in CPython for a complete breakdown.

[1] PEP 703 - Making the Global Interpreter Lock Optional in CPython | peps ...
    https://peps.python.org/pep-0703/
    The GIL is an obstacle to using multi-core CPUs from Python efficiently. This PEP proposes adding a build configuration (--disable-gil) to CPython to let it run Python code without the global interpreter lock and with the necessary changes needed to make the interpreter thread-safe. Motivation The GIL is a major obstacle to concurrency.

[2] PEP 703: Making the Python global interpreter lock optional
    https://lwn.net/Articles/919563/
    A new build configuration flag, --without-gil will be added to the configure script that will build CPython without the global interpreter lock. The posting of a PEP is only one step in a long path toward integrating this change into the CPython interpreter; expect some extended discussions over the coming months.

[3] PEP 703 Explained: How Python Finally Removes the GIL
    https://dev.to/epam_india_python/pep-703-explained-how-python-finally-removes-the-gil-49d
    PEP 703 is one of the most transformative changes in CPython's history. This proposal—now accepted—re-architects memory management, garbage collection, and container safety to safely enable true parallelism. For years, Python has had a massive "elephant in the room": the Global Interpreter Lock (GIL). If you have ever written a Python script that tries to do two CPU-heavy tasks at once ...

[4] PEP 703 - Making the Global Interpreter Lock Optional in CPython - GitHub
    https://github.com/irthomasthomas/undecidability/issues/733
    PEP 703 - Making the Global Interpreter Lock Optional in CPython | peps.python.org DESCRIPTION: CPython's global interpreter lock ("GIL") prevents multiple threads from executing Python code at the same time. [5] PEP 703 Free-Threaded Python: What It Means and When It Lands
    https://codegym.cc/groups/posts/python-pep-703-free-threaded-explained
    The Global Interpreter Lock is the most-discussed limitation of CPython for thirty years. Every "why is threading slow in Python" article points to the GIL. Every workaround (multiprocessing, asyncio, C extensions that release the GIL) exists because of it. In October 2025, the Python 3.14 release made the free-threaded build officially supported via PEP 779, which depended on the architecture ...

[1] PEP 703 – Making the Global Interpreter Lock Optional in CPython
    https://www.linkedin.com/posts/eliot-kmiec_pep-703-making-the-global-interpreter-lock-activity-7271941402740043776-IS5w
    The Global Interpreter Lock (GIL) is now optional, unlocking real multi-core parallelism in pure Python. For decades, the GIL limited Python to a single thread, forcing teams to rely on multiprocessing or external frameworks for CPU-bound workloads.

[2] PEP 703: Making the Python global interpreter lock optional [LWN.net]
    https://lwn.net/Articles/919616/
    > Without changing the API, how do you propose any given Python call know which interpreter it is talking to? A classic solution to this problem is to make the context thread-local. Here, you'd bind each thread to at most one subinterpreter (or to a group of subinterpreters that share a GIL).

[3] Python's Steering Council Plans to Make Its 'Global Interpreter Lock.....
    https://developers.slashdot.org/story/23/07/29/037250/pythons-steering-council-plans-to-make-its-global-interpreter-lock-optional
    Friday the Python Steering Council "announced its intent to accept PEP 703 (Making the Global Interpreter Lock Optional in CPython), with initial support possibly showing up in the 3.13 release," reports LWN.net.

[4] Python 3.13: Disable the GIL to Unlock True Multithreading Power
    https://openillumi.com/en/en-python-3-13-gil-free-multithread/
    The introduction of the optional Global Interpreter Lock (GIL) disabling feature in Python 3.13 (Free-Threading Mode, PEP 703) addresses the long-standing performance bottleneck in CPU-bound multithreaded applications.

    https://peps.python.org/pep-0820/
    This makes it cumbersome to use "optional" features - ones that should only take effect if the interpreter supports them. The recently added slots Py_mod_gil and Py_mod_multiple_interpreters are good examples. One workaround is to check the Python version, and omit slots that predate the current interpreter. This is cumbersome for users.
